metricOrigin: performance.now() plus Runtime.getHeapUsage() around the isolated-world stack

acceptedRegression.reason: Real growth, carried openly and left out of the reference. Measured the same sitting on Chromium 153 with the same watch capture, as first paint min (watch stage min coreLoader / featureModules / monolith): 7f69780d (2026-08-22) 125.70 ms (52.70 / 6.30 / 87.70, 9 modules); 69a67ff6 (2026-09-14) 150.40 ms (60.80 / 12.10 / 91.80, 10 modules); v4.99.2 157.30 ms (68.90 / 11.80 / 92.00, 18 modules); v4.106.0 161.00 ms (78.20 / 14.30 / 81.50, 31 modules). The tree bound for v4.107.0 read 152.90 and 160.20 ms on the 2026-10-31 capture (77.40 / 16.30 / 86.60, 32 modules) and v4.106.0 read 168.70 ms on the same capture, so this release added nothing; the floor rose earlier, in the module-load stages, as code left the monolith. It had used up the whole 25 ms tolerance and read pass or fail on scheduling alone. RATCHET: this number may only decrease, and the 2026-08-22 reference stays the goal. ROADMAP.md carries the work to earn it back.

steadyStateBudget.reason: Idle cost of the DEFAULT feature set on a captured watch/feed page, held open and untouched, measured via CDP Performance.getMetrics (real CPU seconds, no page instrumentation). Observed on the 2026-08-18 reference: script 18.6-27.0 ms/min, task 84.7-88.7 ms/min, 6 layouts and 6 style recalcs per minute. Budgets are ~2x observed: the point is to catch a runaway interval or a layout-thrash loop, not to police jitter. Tighten as the numbers settle. NOTE on idleHeapGrowthBytesPerMin: until 2026-09-05 this metric read the heap without collecting first, so it measured allocation minus whatever GC happened to land inside the ten-second window rather than retention. The 364-386 KB/min recorded here on 2026-08-18 was that older quantity; a busy box reported 6.85 MB/min twice in a row for the same code. The sampler now forces a collection before each reading and the same tree measures 218-238 KB/min of RETAINED growth. The 1500000 budget is deliberately left where it is: it is a runaway-leak ceiling, the self-test proves it catches one at 153 MB/min, and tightening it to ~2x the new observation is a separate decision that should be taken against a quiet-machine reference rather than these numbers. NOTE on the settle: until 2026-11-01 this lane started sampling straight after the startup session and multiplied ten seconds by six, so one-time setup read as a recurring cost. A real sixty-second window on the 2026-10-31 watch capture put every sampled millisecond of script in its first two seconds and none after, for 22.70 ms/min script, 75.83 ms/min task, 2 layouts, 2 style recalcs and 669,543 bytes/min, while the ten-second window read 127.24 ms/min, 255.56 ms/min, 12, 12 and 4,011,744 bytes/min on the same tree. The sampler now waits STEADY_STATE_SETTLE_MS first. The budgets did not move.

history.note: Retained because the 2026-08-18 bisect against it found a REAL ~2x regression, all measured same-machine same-sitting: 3c9a5ef2 49.30 paint / 57.70 parse+init -> 86cac849 59.00/90.40 -> ab1c45a3 86.40/119.20 -> dbd9a75e 109.80/137.00 -> 103.90/134.40 at v4.63.0. Loading the 75-module foundation graph concurrently (b5c933aa) recovered a large part of it. The absolute numbers below are NOT comparable to those, which is why this reference was retired rather than kept and papered over with ever-widening allowances.

history.machine: post-rebuild hardware before the Chrome 151 reference refresh
history.note: The browser version was not recorded with this reference. On Chrome 151.0.7922.138, detached commit 836e9611 measured 196.70 ms parse/init and 134.40 ms paint, while the polished tree measured 187.70 ms and 129.20 ms in the immediately following run. The changed tree was faster, so the old reference was retired as an environment mismatch rather than widened to cover a code regression.
